extracted.intended_audience: screenwriters and authors adapting novels into screenplays
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and practical strategies for converting a novel's narrative, characters, and themes into an economical, visually-driven screenplay or limited-series format while preserving the source's emotional core. Includes structural mapping, visual translation, dialogue transformation, pacing, and collaboration advice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding the Fundamental Shift
rubrics_metrics.description: Film and literature are fundamentally different storytelling mediums; novels use interior monologues and descriptive passages, whereas screenplays require visual narratives and external action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept that adapting isn't merely compressing pages into fewer ones but recreating the tale for a new medium. Example: The Great Gatsby relies on internal observations, so film adaptations must externalize those ideas (e.g., Baz Luhrmann used visual metaphors and stylized cinematography).

rubrics_metrics.name: The Challenge of Compression
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine what to keep and what to cut when a long novel must be reduced for screen; consolidate characters, reduce subplots, and simplify complex tales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compression requires 'surgical accuracy and innovative problem-solving.' Examples: The Lord of the Rings cut Tom Bombadil yet retained epic scope; Game of Thrones condensed storylines by consolidating characters and streamlining political plots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserving the Core Essence
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify and protect the novel's emotional core and central themes rather than slavishly retaining every plot point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structural changes (like reorganizing timelines) are acceptable if they preserve the heart of the story. Example: Greta Gerwig's Little Women preserved the meditation on sisterhood despite timeline reordering; Dune concentrated on the central coming-of-age drama and political intrigue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start with Structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Break down the novel into a basic three-act structure, identifying inciting incident, major plot points, and climax (or create a 'story spine' for complex novels).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the three-act framework as a scaffold for the adaptation. For complex works, outline the essential narrative progression so you can decide what fits within a cinematic arc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify Visual Opportunities
rubrics_metrics.description: Look for moments in the novel that can be transformed into compelling visual sequences; internal struggles must be externalized through action and dialogue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Find cinematic equivalents for literary devices: metaphors become visual motifs, internal monologues become confrontations or visual beats. Seek scenes that can 'show' rather than 'tell.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop a Character Hierarchy
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine primary and secondary characters early and be prepared to combine or eliminate others to fit screen time constraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess which characters serve similar functions and can be merged without losing essential story elements. Prioritizing characters helps preserve central arcs while trimming peripheral material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Find the Cinematic Angle
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide which aspect of the story will be most compelling on screen; this may mean shifting focus from the book's primary narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A faithful adaptation isn't always the best one — choose the cinematic through-line even if it requires significant changes. Example: Apocalypse Now relocated Heart of Darkness to Vietnam while preserving psychological core.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual Translation (Economy and Imagery)
rubrics_metrics.description: Screenplays must be economical and visual: every scene should move the story forward while maintaining atmosphere and tone through action and dialogue alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Find creative ways to convey information originally presented by description. Avoid long expository scenes; use visual motifs, props, locations, and actions to communicate backstory and world-building.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialogue Transformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Literary dialogue often doesn't work directly on screen and must be reimagined to be more immediate and dramatic while preserving its essential purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine multiple conversations into one scene, create new dialogue that expresses what narration did, and sharpen beats for cinematic clarity and emotional immediacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pacing and Rhythm
rubrics_metrics.description: Screen stories move at a different pace than written ones; adapters must maintain momentum while allowing space for reflection and character development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reorganize events to create dynamic sequences and stronger dramatic arcs; balance forward motion with quieter moments to preserve tone without losing audience engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honor the Source While Creating an Independent Film
rubrics_metrics.description: The goal is not to replicate the book exactly but to create a new work that honors its source while standing independently as a film.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This may include stripping subplots, modifying elements, or adding original scenes that enhance cinematic impact. Example: The Godfather removed many subplots and added iconic scenes to produce a film that stands on its own.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaboration and Compromise
rubrics_metrics.description: Adaptation involves multiple stakeholders (authors, producers, directors, studio officials); managing relationships and compromises is essential while maintaining creative integrity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop strong communication skills and be able to articulate why certain changes are necessary to build trust with protective stakeholders. Successful adaptations are typically collaborative efforts that consider source content and new-media needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format Selection and Leveraging New Platforms
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose the appropriate format (feature film vs limited series) and leverage new technologies and platform opportunities when adapting complex novels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Streaming and limited-series formats can allow more complete adaptations of complex works; new technologies offer innovative visualization options. Examples: Station Eleven and Normal People used serialized formats to retain nuance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artistic Vision Combined with Technical Expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: Successful adaptation requires respect for the source material, technical screenplay craft, and an overarching artistic vision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance fidelity to theme and emotional core with technical concerns (visual storytelling, pacing, format). Use tools and processes (e.g., character mapping, visual narrative planning) to streamline adaptation while preserving creativity.
